planting.note: Mount on bark, driftwood, or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; bulb air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering.

directions: Mount on bark, driftwood, or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; bulb air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering. A distinctive, bulbous, onion-like base of tightly curled, silvery-green, twisting leaves gives this small epiphyte an almost octopus-like or squid-like appearance unlike the straighter, more open forms of many other air plants, with a spike of small violet flowers emerging from bright red bracts when mature. Native to Central American and Caribbean forests, where it grows perched on tree branches absorbing moisture and nutrients through specialized leaf scales, it thrives with a thorough soak or misting two to three times a week followed by good air circulation to dry the base and prevent rot. Provide bright, filtered light rather than direct sun, and remove the mother plant's offsets (pups) once they reach about half the parent's size to propagate.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Mount on bark, driftwood, or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Medusa's Head air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering.

directions: Mount on bark, driftwood, or display unpotted in bright, indirect light with good air circulation; Medusa's Head air plant grows without soil and needs regular misting or soaking rather than traditional watering. A swollen, bulbous base sends out numerous long, twisting, silvery-scaled leaves that curl and writhe outward in every direction, evoking the mythological gorgon and giving the plant its dramatic common name, with a brilliant spike of red bracts and violet-blue flowers appearing from the leaf tips at maturity. Native to Central American and Mexican forests and scrublands, it tolerates brighter light and somewhat drier conditions than many soft-leaved tillandsias, reflecting its more xeric native habitat compared to rainforest air plants. Soak or mist thoroughly two to three times weekly, shake off excess water to prevent rot in the tightly curled base, and provide bright light for the best form and most reliable flowering.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; Sapphire Tower is a Chilean mountain bromeliad that tolerates light frost once established but needs excellent drainage year-round.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; Sapphire Tower is a Chilean mountain bromeliad that tolerates light frost once established but needs excellent drainage year-round. Rosettes of stiff, silvery, spine-edged leaves send up a dramatic, sometimes six-foot flower spike after several years of growth, studded with an extraordinary, luminous blue-green to turquoise flower color unlike almost any other hardy plant, with contrasting bright orange pollen-bearing anthers. Native to rocky slopes in the Chilean Andes, it is a terrestrial bromeliad rather than an epiphyte, rooting into gritty mountain soil, and is prized in xeriscape and Mediterranean-climate gardens for its unique flower color and architectural, spiny rosette form. It flowers only once per rosette after reaching maturity, then produces offsets at the base before the flowering rosette declines, so leave the spent rosette in place until offsets are established.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; star flower cactus rots quickly in wet or dense soil and prefers to dry out fully between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; star flower cactus rots quickly in wet or dense soil and prefers to dry out fully between waterings. Fleshy, toothed, four-angled stems sprawl and clump low to the ground, producing large, star-shaped flowers mottled in yellow and maroon-brown with a wrinkled, fleshy texture that mimics rotting flesh, an adaptation that attracts fly pollinators and gives the plant its common carrion-flower associations, along with a correspondingly unpleasant scent when in bloom. Native to South Africa's Eastern Cape, it is a low-growing, clustering succulent well suited to a succulent dish garden, hanging container, or rock garden pocket, where its unusual flowers provide a conversation-starting bloom several times a year. Site the pot away from windows and doors when flowering to avoid the odor indoors, and water only when the soil is completely dry.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty potting mix; parachute plant stores water in its succulent stems and tubers and prefers to dry out between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty potting mix; parachute plant stores water in its succulent stems and tubers and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thin, wiry, trailing succulent stems bear pairs of small heart-shaped leaves and unusual, pale green flowers shaped like a tiny umbrella or parachute, complete with a fringe of fine hairs around the rim that trap small fly pollinators temporarily inside the flower before releasing them dusted in pollen. Native to South Africa, it grows from a small underground tuber that stores water and energy through dry periods, and its slender trailing stems make it a good candidate for a small hanging basket where its odd, whimsical flowers can be seen up close. Water only when the potting mix is fully dry, provide bright indirect light, and avoid overpotting this slow-growing tuberous vine.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Fluffy Ruffles Boston fern wants higher humidity than average indoor air and benefits from regular misting.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Fluffy Ruffles Boston fern wants higher humidity than average indoor air and benefits from regular misting. This dense, compact sport of the classic Boston fern produces heavily divided, finely ruffled, densely overlapping fronds that give the whole plant a plush, feathery texture quite different from the longer, more open fronds of standard Boston fern, staying more compact and upright rather than trailing dramatically. Its bushier, less pendulous habit makes it a good choice for a tabletop or pedestal display as well as a hanging basket, and it shares the classic Boston fern's air-purifying reputation and easy care once its humidity needs are met. Keep the potting mix consistently moist, provide humidity through misting or a pebble tray, and trim any browned fronds at the base.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Pink Silver hoya colors most vividly in bright indirect light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, chunky potting mix; Pink Silver hoya colors most vividly in bright indirect light and blooms most reliably when slightly pot-bound. Narrow, dusky green leaves are heavily speckled with silvery flecks and flush pink to burgundy along the margins in bright light, growing on vigorous, twining vines that produce rounded clusters of small, dark maroon-pink, fuzzy-centered flowers with a musky, spicy fragrance most noticeable at night. A popular, fast-growing selection of one of the most variable hoya species, it tolerates a wider range of indoor conditions than many finer hoyas and rewards a sunny window with abundant, repeat blooms from the same flowering spurs. Provide a trellis or moss pole for climbing, let the potting mix dry between waterings, and never remove the woody flower spurs, which rebloom for years.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Direct sow into wet, saline mud or sand at the tidal margin in full sun; dwarf glasswort is a true halophyte adapted to regular tidal flooding with salt water and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone.

directions: Direct sow into wet, saline mud or sand at the tidal margin in full sun; dwarf glasswort is a true halophyte adapted to regular tidal flooding with salt water and will not thrive in ordinary garden soil or fresh water alone. Leafless, jointed, bright green succulent stems form dense colonies along salt marsh and tidal flat margins, turning red as they mature in fall, and the crisp, salty, juicy young stem tips are harvested and eaten raw or lightly cooked as a gourmet vegetable known variously as sea bean, sea asparagus, or samphire greens. Unlike the perennial glassworts, this annual species completes its life cycle in a single season, germinating on bare tidal mud in spring and setting seed by fall, making it useful both as a foraged coastal vegetable and as a candidate crop for experimental saline agriculture research irrigated with seawater. It requires the specific conditions of a real tidal or brackish marsh edge to thrive and is not a candidate for a typical home garden setting away from the coast.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
